author: Émile Zola
introFa: کتاب «Germinal» نوشته Émile Zola یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.

واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: Develop., Growth and Differ., 24 (2), 205-215 (1982) A Possibility of an in Vitro Differentiation of Primordial Germ Cells (PGCs) from Blastomeres Containing “Germinal Plasm” of Early Cleavage Stage in Xenopus Zaevis (xenopus laevis/“germinal plasm”/germinal granule/PGCs) KOHJI IKENISHI Department of Biology, Faculty of Science, Osaka City University, Sugimoto. Sumiyoshi-ku, Osaka 558, Japan. The blastomeres containing the “germinal plasm” were isolated from 32-cell stage Xenopus embryos and cultured in vitro for various poriods of time till the control embryos developed to stage 28, 33/34, 40 and 45, respectively. The cells containing the plasm in the ‘stage-28’, ‘33/34’ and ‘40’ explants were similar in external shape, and in distribution in the spherical endodermal cell mass to the presumptive primordial germ cells (pPGCs) in normal embryos of the corresponding stages. In addition, the cells in explants as well as the pPGCs were separated by a large intercellular space from the surrounding endodermal cells. The change in proportion of the compact or the loosely struc- tured germinal granules and the irregularly shaped-stringlike bodies (ISBs) occurred in the cells of the explants with the prolongation of the culture period. In the cells of the ‘stage-45’ explant as well as in the PGCs of normal stage-45 tadpoles the ISBs and “granular materials” replace those germinal granules. These facts lead to the conclusion that the change of the germinal granules through the ISBs, to the “granular materials”, noticed in the normal course of differentiation of pPGCs into PGCs (see (l)), also takes place in the cells of the explants during the culture. Therefore, it is likely that the cells in the explants are genuine pPGCs or PGCs. This is the first demonstration of a possibility of the in vitro differentiatim of PGCs from the blastomeres containing the “germinal plasm” of early cleavage stage. Since a discovery of “germinal plasm” in Rana temporaria (2) many investigators have confirmed in various anuran species that the plasm plays an important role in the formation of PGCs (for review, see (3)). The plasm located at the vegetal pole region of unfertilized eggs is incorporated into some blastomeres at the cleavage stages, which differentiate into PGCs at the tadpole stages. Above all, SMITH (4) has demonstrated a determinative role of the vegetal pole cytoplasm, perhaps the “germinal plasm”, in the restoration of PGCs in the uv-irradiated Rana pipiens embryos which had been complete sterile, by injecting the vegetal pole cytoplasm from unirradiated eggs. WAKAHARA (5) has also shown by means of microinjection that certain fractions of the vegetal pole cytoplasm possess a PGC-forming activity in uv-irradiated Rana chensinensis. However, direct evidence that the “germinal plasm” is germ cell determinant could be obtained through the demonstration that the somatic cells into which the plasm is injected (recipient cells) differentiate into functional germ cells, as shown in Drosophila (6, 7). It seems to be difficult to show such transdetermination in anurans because of the difficulty is identifying the recipient cells externally from the morphological features in the developing embryos and of long generation time as compared with Drosophila. 205

206 K. IKENISHI It is almost undoubted from grafting experiments between genetically marked embryos (8, 9, 10, 11, 12) that the functional gamates of Xenopus are derived solely from PGCs. There- fore, it may be possible to replace a subject of the formation of functional germ cells from the recipient cells with that of PGCs from the recipient cells. To test whether the recipient cells differentiate into PGCs in Xenopus or to know a role of “germinal plasm” in transdetermination, in vitro system may be much advantageous in contrast with in vivo system. Because in the former it is possible to know directly whether the PGCs can be derived from the recipient cells or not, and we need not think about many factors other than the “germinal plasm” which may have something to do with the process of germ cell formation in the latter. However, the in vitro differentiation of anuran PGCs has not been reported so far. It is firstly necessary to investigate a possibility that the cells originally containing the plasm at cleavage stages differentiate into PGCs in vitro. In order to clarify the in vitro differentiation of PGCs, the blastomeres containing the plasm were isolated from 32-cell stage (stage 6) Xenopus embryos and allowed to differentiate in culture for various periods of time. The reason why the stage-6 embryos were chosen is as follows. The blastomeres are always situated around the vegetal pole at that stage, so that they are easily identified externally. The degree of differentiation was estimated from the ultrastructural features of the germinal granule restricted in the “germinal plasm” which was considered to show a stage-specific morphology (1). MATERIALS AND METHODS Fertilized eggs of Xenopus luevis were obtained by injecting gonadotropic hormone into sexually mature males and females as reported elsewhere (13). Embryos at the 2- to 4- cell stage were placed in 1-2% sodium thioglycollate (Nakarai Chemicals Ltd.) in 10% Holtfreter solution adjusted to pH 9-10 with NaOH for 1-2 min at room temperature (22-24°C) to remove the jelly coat. Dejellied embryos were rinsed three or four times with sterile distilled water containing 100 ,ug/ml kanamycin sulfate. Some of the embryos were allowed to develop to the tadpole stage (stage 45) at 22~tO.5”C to make the control group. The rest were transferred to sterile conditions, in which all subsequent procedures were carried out. Embryos were placed in 1/15 M Sorensen phosphate buffer (pH 7.3) to dissociate the blas- tomeres. At stage 6, four blastomeres around the vegetal pole of the lowest tier, known to contain the “germinal plasm” and larger than other blastomeres, were isolated by means of a hair needle and a hair loop. Location of the blastomeres containing the plasm was checked in advance in light microscopic sections (Fig. 1). Isolated blastomeres were transferred to agar-bottomed glass culture dishes containing either 10% foetal calf serum in full strength Holtfreter solution buffered to pH 7.3 with HEPES or Liebovitz medium (50% Liebovitz’s L-15 medium, 40% distilled water and 10% foetal calf serum (15)), both of which containing 100 ,ug/ml kanamycin sulfate. Blastomeres were cultured for various periods of time at 22~t0.5”C till the control embryos reached stages 28, 33/34, 40 and 45, respectively. The explants and control tadpoles were fixed with modified Karnovsky solution, postfixed with osmium and embedded in Epoxy resin as described elsewhere (16). Cultured cells containing “germinal plasm” were identified based on the criteria used in the previous study (16), and were compared light and electron micro- scopically with pPGCs in normal embryos of the corresponding stages in the previous studies (1, 17) or PGCs of normal tadpoles. Sections were made with a Porter-Blum MT-2B ultramicrotome, stained with uranyl acetate and lead citrate, and viewed in an electron microscope (JEM-100U or Hitachi H-300). The degree of differentiation was judged from ultrastructural features of the germinal granules which were considered to change with development (cf. (l)), i. e., compact germinal granules transform via loosely structured germinal granules and ISBs to “granular materials”. Germinal granules are never observed in the PGCs of tadpoles beyond stage 40, where ISBs and “granular materials” are found. Embryos were staged after NIEUWKOOP and FABER (14).

In advanced explants (‘stage-33/34’, ‘40’ and ‘45’ explants) they are principally roundish and separately located from each other on or near the peripheral part (Fig. 3). Some of them have a large cytoplasmic process (Fig. 4) and are bounded by long filopodia of the surrounding endodermal cells, which are separated by a large intercellular space. The cells containing the plasm decreased in size as the culture period was prolonged (Figs. 2 and 3), like the pPGCs did with development (1, 18). In ‘stage-45’ explant they are considerably larger with more yolk platelets in the cytoplasm as compared with the PGCs, being roundish, in the genital ridges of the normal tadpoles (Figs. 3 and 5). The cells containing the “germinal plasm” in the explant were mainly composed of a lot of mitochondria and the plasm-specific germinal granules or their derivatives. In addition, numerous free ribosomes and glycogen granules, lipid droplets, yolk platelets, cortical granules (l9), pigment granules and so on were recognized in the cytoplasm. Thus, there is no difference in cytoplasmic component between the cells of the explant and the pPGCs or the PGCs of the normal embryos. As far as the ultrastructural feature of the germinal granule is concerned, the compact or the loosely structured germinal granules (Figs. 6 and 7) and ISBs (Fig. 8) were always observed in the cells containing the plasm of the ‘stage- 28’, ‘33/34’ and ‘40’ explants (Fig. 10). As the culture period was prolonged the ISBs were more often found while the compact germinal granules were less recognized (Fig. 10). In the ‘stage-45’ explant the germinal granules were never observed. Instead, the ISBs are frequently seen in the proximity of the nucleus and the “granular materials” (Fig. 9) are sometimes found among mitochondria. Both organelles are also noticed in the PGCs situated in the genital ridges of the normal stage-45 tadpoles. DISCUSSION In the present study, the cells containing the “germinal plasm” are observed in all explants, which were cultured for various periods of time (Table 1). The features of the cells in the explants are similar to the pPGCs in normal embryos of the corresponding stages. Above all, the changes of the cells in external shape, and in location and a manner of clustering in the spherical endodermal cell mass during the ‘stages 28-33/34‘ are in good agreement with those of the pPGCs, which were thought to be related with the active migration during the corresponding stages (17). That is, the cells change their external shape from polygonal into roundish during those stages (Figs. 2 and 3), but the somatic endodermal cells remain polygonal. At the same time, the cells which have been closely aggregated forming one cluster in somewhat inner part, where is not so far from the periphery, of the ‘stage-28’ explant come to be separately located from each other in peripheral region of the advanced explants (‘stage-33/34‘, ‘40’ and ‘45’ explants) (Figs. 2 and 3). Besides, the cells of the advanced explants are also surrounded by long filopodia of the endodermal cells which are separated by a large intercellular space (Fig. 4), as noticed on the pPGCs of the migratory period (18). From an ultrastructural analysis, the compact or the loosely structured germinal granules and the ISBs are present in the cells containing the plasm of the ‘stage-28’, ‘33/34’ and ‘40’ explants (Figs. 6, 7, 8 and 10). However, the proportion of these three types in the cells is changed with culture period, i.e., the ISRs are more often observed but the compact germinal granules are less recognized with prolongation of the culture period (Fig. 10). Such a tendency in the cells of the explant has already been reported in the pPGCs of normal embryos with development (Fig. 10) (1). In the cells containing the plasm of the ‘stage-45’ explant as well as in the PGCs of the normal stage-45 tadpole, the compact or the loosely structured germinal granules are no longer found, and the ISBs and the “granular materials” (Fig. 9) replace those granules. Therefore, it is plausible that the change of the germinal granules through the ISBs to the “granular materials” also takes place in the cells of the explants during the culture. The facts mentioned above strongly suggest that the cells containing the “germinal plasm” in the explants are genuine pPGCs or PGCs. It, therefore, turns out that the cells which are quite similar in morphological features at both light and electron microscopic levels to PGCs have been originated in vitro from the blastomeres containing the plasm isolated at early cleavage stage. The PGCs in the ‘stage-45’ explant are bigger than those of normal stage-45 tadpoles, having more yolk platelets inside (Figs. 3 and 5). This indicates a delay in the differentiation process

214 K. IKENISHI of these PGCs as compared with normal ones, for the yolk content in PGCs decreases with development. The idea of delay is also supported by the fact that the nucleus of the PGCs in the explant is less indented than that of normal tadpoles (Figs. 3 and 5), because indentation of the nucleus becomes deeper as development proceeds (1). Anyway, the PGCs in the ‘stage-45’ explant have differentiated to at least PGCs corresponding to those in normal tadpoles of stage 40 or older, since the compact or the loosely structured germinal granules are no longer found and the ISBs and the “granular materials” replace those germinal granules. There is a wide variety in the number of pPGCs or PGCs found in the explant of the same culture period, especially in ‘stage-40’ and ‘45’ explants. The number seems to be related to the size of the explant (Table l), which may depend on the degree of cell damage during isolation at stage 6. If the isolation is carried out well, a lot of PGCs might be found. Twenty-nine PGCs which were found in one explant, nearly the average number of normal controls (Table l), suggests such a situation. It is well known that the inductive influence is essential for the differentiation of various tissues and organs in Amphibiu. In urodeles, the PGCs are demonstrated to be derived from common totipotent cells of the presumptive ectoderm under an inductive influence of the endoderm (20). In the present study, the cells which are indistinguishable in morphological features from PGCs are diffrentiated from the blastomeres containing the “germinal plasm” of the cleavage stage, which normally comprise a part of the presumptive endoderm (21). Moreover, neither mesodermal nor ectodermal tissues and organs are recognized even in the ‘stage-45’ explant, and any endodermal tissue is also not differentiated (Fig. 3). This implies that the inductive influences from the germ layers other than the endoderm is not necessary for the in vitro differentiation of the cells, possibly PGCs, in Xenopus. Therefore, by the introduction of the “germinal plasm” in the present in vitro system it may be possible to transdetermine somatic blastomeres into PGCs, at least from a morphological point of view.
